clue.text: A most note-worthy and harmonious celebration, of course

definitions.text: A most note-worthy and harmonious celebration, of course

parts.words: A most note-worthy and harmonious celebration, of course
parts.note: note-worthy puns on musical notes and harmonious on harmony; the event is a celebration of music held over a course of days

explanation.surface: A remarkable, friendly party that naturally went well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note-worthy' and 'harmonious' read as praise for any party, but both point at music.
explanation.definitionFit: A festival devoted to concerts is literally full of notes and harmony, and runs as a programme of events.

clue.text: Characteristic of every old maid

parts.note: an old maid is a woman who never married, so the trait shared by all of them is never having taken a husband

explanation.surface: A trait common to all elderly spinsters.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinster by definition has never married, so this unmarried state is her one universal trait.

clue.text: Meanwhile put 'im down among the dead men

indicators.note: the clue puts the pronoun beside the burial phrase, so it is placed after that verb in the answer

parts.note: to lay someone in the grave among the dead is to inter them
dropped-aitch spelling of him, as written in the clue

explanation.surface: A grim order to bury someone in the meantime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put 'im down' sounds like a cockney order, read as INTER + 'IM.
explanation.definitionFit: A temporary arrangement lasting in the meantime; as an adverb it means in the interval.

clue.text: This might be useful in cases of naturalization

definitions.text: This might be useful in cases of naturalization

parts.words: This might be useful in cases of naturalization
parts.note: a person taking new nationality exchanges a foreign allegiance for a new one; the phrase also means currency trading across borders

explanation.surface: Advice about what helps when becoming a citizen of a new country.
explanation.walkthrough: Naturalization swaps one nationality for another, a foreign swap; the answer's usual sense is buying other countries' money.
explanation.definitionFit: Changing citizenship is literally swapping something abroad for something at home, which the currency-market phrase describes.

clue.text: Where middlemen appropriately profit

parts.note: retailers are middlemen between maker and buyer, and a retail precinct is in the middle of town, so men in the middle trade in the middle

explanation.surface: A question of where wholesalers and dealers make their money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriately' flags the joke: middlemen do business in places named for the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Retail precincts are the central places where traders between producer and customer make their margins.

clue.text: Substitute word for " at home " ?

parts.note: at home is IN, and a stead is a homestead or place, so the phrase reads 'in place'; the word itself means as a substitute

explanation.surface: Looking for a synonym for the phrase 'at home'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At home' gives IN and a stead is a dwelling place (as in farmstead), so the answer reads 'in house'; its real meaning is 'as a substitute'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb meaning in place of something else is the very word one uses to signal a substitute.

clue.text: "— voices prophesying war" (Coleridge)

parts.note: a line from Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan, where the khan hears from far voices of his forefathers foretelling war

explanation.surface: A quotation to complete from a Romantic poet.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash stands for the missing word of the line from 'Kubla Khan': '... voices prophesying war'.
explanation.definitionFit: The voices in the poem belong to the khan's forebears, so the missing adjective means of one's forefathers.

clue.text: It makes Ida yell

indicators.note: the answer's letters make up the two words Ida yell, so those words are a reshuffle of it

explanation.surface: Something that causes a woman named Ida to shout.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate definition: 'It' is the answer, and 'makes' says its letters rearranged spell IDA YELL. The clue is a teasing pure anagram, typical of the 1950s.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in a perfect world, and the clue relies on its letters alone rather than any synonym.

clue.text: Got the pip ?

parts.note: 'to have the pip' is old British slang for feeling unwell or out of sorts; a fruit with pips is full of seeds

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone is feeling off colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The pip' is British slang for feeling poorly or fed up; literally a pip is a fruit seed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both shabby and off-colour, and also full of pips, so both readings of the question fit.

clue.text: Whither progress is by rolling

parts.note: alludes to the Kipling song from the Just So Stories whose singer longs to go rolling south to a Brazilian port city

explanation.surface: A philosophical question about where rolling progress leads.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue turns on Rudyard Kipling's poem 'Rolling Down to Rio' from the Just So Stories, so the destination of the rolling is the title's last words.
explanation.definitionFit: In Kipling's verse the rolling journey leads southward to the Brazilian port, so the phrase names that destination.

clue.text: It might be close at the foot of the column

definitions.text: at the foot of the column
definitions.note: a plain block set beneath a column or pedestal; the clue phrase describes where it sits rather than naming it

indicators.note: says these letters might be something else once rearranged, signalling a reshuffle of the word close

explanation.surface: Something is near the base of a pillar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It might be close' reads as nearness, but 'might be' tells you to rearrange CLOSE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plinth-like base block supports a column, so it is found at the column's foot.

clue.text: A man who cannot exist without some corporation

definitions.text: A man who cannot exist without some corporation

parts.words: A man who cannot exist without some corporation
parts.note: a civic officer of a borough council exists only as part of a municipal corporation; corporation also jokes on a paunch; the tree name plus man makes his title

explanation.surface: A man who depends on belonging to a company or a big belly.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a tree; add MAN and you get the council officer the clue describes, whose office needs a borough corporation (and, in cartoons, a stout 'corporation' or paunch).
explanation.definitionFit: The tree word joined to 'man' names a senior councillor, who exists only within a town's governing body.

clue.text: Forced to serve by being stamped on

definitions.meaning: sailors seized by the press gang were pressed into naval service against their will
a mark pressed into a surface has been stamped on it

explanation.surface: Someone bullied into service by being trodden on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By being' is only a link joining the two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both conscription by a press gang and a design printed or embossed by pressure.

clue.text: The shoemaker goes in to bat

definitions.text: The shoemaker goes in to bat

parts.words: The shoemaker goes in to bat
parts.note: a shoemaker works on a last, a foot-shaped block, so he is a man of the last; in cricket the final batter of an innings is the one who goes in last

explanation.surface: A cobbler takes his turn at the crease in a cricket match.
explanation.walkthrough: A last is a cobbler's foot-shaped form; in cricket the batting order ends with the tenth-wicket player, who goes in last.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names both the cobbler (whose tool is a last) and the final cricketer to walk out and bat.

clue.text: A blow to a desperate stake at arm's length

definitions.note: where this item sits: at the end of a sleeve, at the full length of the arm

parts.note: a gambler in despair bets his shirt, the last thing he owns
a cuff is a slap or blow with the hand

explanation.surface: A gambler's desperate bet is struck a blow while kept at a distance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At arm's length' reads as keeping aloof, but means at the wrist end of a sleeve; 'to' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: The band at the end of a sleeve sits at the wrist, the far end of the arm.

clue.text: Right at the bottom of the drain

definitions.note: the lowest point of anything; a noun phrase as the answer is a noun

indicators.note: to right something is to set it straight, so the letters of drain are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Something lies right down at the base of a drainpipe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right at the bottom' reads as an intensifier, but 'Right' is the instruction to rearrange DRAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The astronomical term for the point directly beneath an observer is used generally for the lowest point.

clue.text: It's best for the present to let them be themselves

definitions.text: It's best for the present to let them be themselves

parts.words: It's best for the present to let them be themselves
parts.note: alludes to the proverb advising that past grievances be let go, letting what is past stay past for the sake of the present

explanation.surface: Advice to let people be who they are for now.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'let ... be ...', repeating the answer; 'the present' contrasts with things past.
explanation.definitionFit: Things past and done with are what the proverb tells us to forgive and forget.

clue.text: Necessary finger for those who require references

definitions.text: Necessary finger for those who require references

parts.words: Necessary finger for those who require references
parts.note: the pointing finger is called by the same name as the alphabetical list of references at the back of a book, which a researcher needs

explanation.surface: Someone seeking references needs a finger to point with.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses meet: the forefinger beside the thumb, and the alphabetical list a reader consults to find references.
explanation.definitionFit: The forefinger shares its name with the back-of-book list that points readers to pages.

clue.text: Not, however, where the engine driver gets draught beer

definitions.text: Not, however, where the engine driver gets draught beer

parts.words: Not, however, where the engine driver gets draught beer
parts.note: the coupling bar by which a locomotive pulls its train is named as if it were a pub bar where beer is drawn

explanation.surface: A warning that the train driver's pint is not served here.
explanation.walkthrough: Beer is drawn at a bar, but the locomotive's bar is the coupling that draws the train.
explanation.definitionFit: The rigid coupling on a locomotive or tractor that pulls a load is a towing bar, not a pub counter.

clue.text: They charge on horse-power

parts.note: mounted soldiers charge at the enemy riding horses; horse-power sounds like an engine rating

explanation.surface: Something billed by its engine rating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charge' suggests a fee or electricity and 'horse-power' an engine, but these are troops attacking on horseback.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounted troops make their attacks powered by actual horses.

clue.text: Direction for singing quavers, perhaps

parts.note: a musical instruction asks a singer to waver the pitch; quavers suggests the eighth notes but means trembling tones

explanation.surface: A score's instruction on how to sing eighth notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quavers' look like the notes (eighth notes in US usage) but mean tremulous wobbles of the voice.
explanation.definitionFit: This Italian musical term instructs a pulsating, wavering tone, which is exactly a quavering voice.

clue.text: "Those move easiest who have learned to — " (Pope)

definitions.text: "Those move easiest who have learned to — " (Pope)

parts.words: "Those move easiest who have learned to — " (Pope)
parts.note: from Alexander Pope's Essay on Criticism: true ease in writing comes from art, as those move easiest who have learned to step in time to music

explanation.surface: A quotation to complete from Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: Pope's couplet: 'True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, / As those move easiest who have learn'd to ...'; the rhyme with 'chance' confirms it.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the art of moving rhythmically to music, which Pope offers as the model of learned ease.

clue.text: Volga lambskin

definitions.meaning: a Russian city lies at the mouth of the Volga river by the Caspian Sea
the curled fleece of young karakul lambs, named after that city

explanation.surface: A sheepskin from the region of Russia's great river.
explanation.definitionFit: The city on the lower Volga gave its name to the tightly curled fur of karakul lambs traded there.

clue.text: Nothing more than the merest coin, yet enough for a celebration

indicators.note: placed after, as something extra beyond the coin, so the zero follows it

parts.note: in British slang 'not a bean' means not a penny, so a bean is the tiniest coin
zero, the round letter O

explanation.surface: Having almost no money is still enough to throw a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A bean is old British slang for a coin ('I haven't a bean'), and a beano is British slang for a jolly party.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a festive spree or knees-up, originally a works outing with a feast.

clue.text: Girl who was not a hit

definitions.note: a shot that fails is a miss; as one word the answer means wrong or awry

parts.note: a young unmarried woman, addressed as Miss

explanation.surface: A young woman who never found success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Who was' is a link; the answer read as one word means wrongly, a failure to hit the mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Going wrong is failing to hit the target, so something gone awry is off the mark.

clue.text: Uncraved by lovesick merryman

parts.note: Gilbert and Sullivan's song 'I have a song to sing, O' tells of a merryman, moping mum, who sipped no sup and craved no morsel of bread as he sighed for a lady

explanation.surface: Something a heartsick jester had no appetite for.
explanation.walkthrough: The source is the duet in 'The Yeomen of the Guard': the merryman 'sipped no sup, and craved no ...' as he sighed for the love of a ladye.
explanation.definitionFit: The lyric names a tiny morsel of bread as the thing the lovelorn jester did not crave.

clue.text: Arrive shortly in native location

indicators.note: one word set inside another: the short form of arrive goes within native

parts.note: taken as written
arr. is the timetable abbreviation for arrive

explanation.surface: A traveller will soon reach their birthplace.
explanation.walkthrough: ARR (the timetable abbreviation for 'arrive') goes in NATIVE after its second letter; 'location' only says where. There is no separate definition: the whole clue hints at a story of coming home.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale of someone's homecoming is a story or account, which is what the whole clue loosely sketches.

clue.text: Is the printer's frame-up on my behalf?

definitions.meaning: the metal frame in which a printer locks up set type for the press
done for the speaker, two words run together

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a printer's conspiracy was set up for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frame-up' suggests a plot, but here it is the printer's frame of locked-up type.
explanation.definitionFit: The printing term for a chase of locked type is spelt like the two words meaning 'for my sake'.

clue.text: Halts in reverse rashly ?

definitions.note: playful: in the form of a rash, so the definition hints at skin blemishes, a plural noun

indicators.note: running backwards, so the word for halts is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: comes to a halt, or stations where trains halt: stops

explanation.surface: Someone stops by backing up recklessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rashly' looks like 'recklessly' but means 'in the form of a rash'; 'in reverse' turns STOPS around.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash shows as blemishes on the skin, so a rash appears as these marks.
